# Shepherd of Hermas Chapter 64 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)

**Translator:** SOPHIA | **Source:** P.Mich. 130, Shepherd of Hermas 64 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-EC/SHE_064_page_001.jpg

---

## Council Notes

Similitude 6 introduces the Two Shepherds — the angel of luxury and deception (*angelos tēs tryphe kai apatēs*) and the angel of punishment (*angelos tēs timōrias*), who will be the subject of chapters 65-76. The contrast between the fine-looking shepherd (luxury/deception) and the rough-looking shepherd (punishment) is deliberately paradoxical: the attractive shepherd is the dangerous one.

The angel of luxury is described as working through desire and self-deception. His victims think they are doing good while doing evil — this is *apatē* (deception) at its most insidious. The mechanism is internal: desires are implanted, pleasures are manufactured, and the person's judgment is corrupted.

The statement in 64:4 — "certain things seem righteous but in the sight of the Lord they are sins" — is Hermas's version of the Proverbs warning: "There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way to death" (Prov 14:12 LXX).

EMET's "grievous appearance" and LOGOS's "downcast appearance" render *phaulos*; SOPHIA uses "downcast" — *phaulos* in later Greek can mean bad/mean/downcast.

---

## Similitude 6, Part 2 — The Two Shepherds

**64:1** He showed me two shepherds. One was dressed in fine clothing, had a fair complexion, and a handsome body; the other was thin, with a dark complexion and rough clothing and a downcast appearance. And he said to me: "Do you see these shepherds?"

**64:2** "I see them, lord," I replied. "The fine one," he said, "is the angel of luxury and deception. He destroys the souls of the servants of God and turns them away from truth, beguiling them with evil desires in which they shall perish. For they forget the commandments of the living God and walk in vain deceptions and the pride of this life; and they are destroyed by this angel — some to death, others to the corruption of their lives."

**64:3** "Lord," I said, "I do not understand how this angel of luxury destroys the souls of people." "Listen," he said. "When any of the servants of God entertains a desire to live in luxury or in deceit, and sets before himself vain and empty desires, this angel of deception who is with him fills the man's heart with great desires, implanting empty pleasures in him — and the man supposes himself to be doing good, when in fact he is doing evil. When therefore this man is satisfied, he is filled with great blindness regarding what he has done."

**64:4** "Lord," I said, "I still do not understand these things about the angel of luxury." "Listen further," he said. "Of all the things a man does in his life, certain things seem righteous in his own eyes, but in the sight of the Lord they are reckoned as sins. Thus the man who supposes he has done good — he has done nothing righteous in the Lord's sight. And in this way every sin appears sweet and pleasurable in the life of this world, so that the servants of God are corrupted."

---

*SOPHIA represents the consensus rendering of EMET, LOGOS, and PNEUMA, with rulings recorded in the Disagreement Log.*
